problem: The positive-real test is incomplete. A rational Z(s) with real coefficients and Re Z(jω) ≥ 0 for all ω can still have a pole in the right half-plane and be non-passive. The standard PR definition also requires no poles in Re s > 0, equivalently Re Z(s) ≥ 0 for Re s > 0.
fix: State the two standard conditions as: Z(s) is real for real s, and Re Z(s) ≥ 0 for all Re s > 0. Then add that for a rational function this is equivalent to no right-half-plane poles plus Re Z(jω) ≥ 0 on the jω axis.

problem: The pole-zero location rules are stated too absolutely. An LC impedance may have a pole at infinity, for example Z(s)=sL. An RC impedance may have a pole at s=0, as the chapter's own K0/s term shows, and may have a zero at infinity. As written, these valid one-ports fail the stated tests.
fix: Say that finite nonzero poles and zeros lie on the jω axis for LC and on the negative real axis for RC. Allow the standard origin and infinity exceptions: LC may have a pole or zero at infinity; RC impedance may have a pole at s=0 and a zero at infinity.

problem: The answer is wrong. Z(s)=(s²+4)/(s(s²+1)) has poles at 0 and ±j1, and zeros at ±j2. On the positive jω axis the order is pole at 0, pole at 1, zero at 2, so they do not alternate. Its partial fractions give Z(s)=4/s − 3s/(s²+1), with a negative residue, so it is not an LC impedance. It is the reciprocal of the worked-example LC impedance, hence an LC admittance.
fix: Answer: No. The poles and zeros do not alternate; two poles occur before the first zero. Also the residue at ±j1 is negative, so it fails the residue test.

problem: The explanation says alternation keeps Re Z(jω) from becoming negative. For an LC impedance, Re Z(jω)=0 at all non-pole frequencies, so this does not explain alternation.
fix: Say that for a reactance function the Foster residues must be positive and the reactance slope must be positive; these conditions force simple poles and zeros to interlace on the jω axis.
